questions.stem: A pathologist examines a surgically resected pituitary tumour under a microscope. The tumour comprises sheets of monomorphic, round to polygonal cells with central nuclei and sparse to absent reticulin network. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A pathologist examines a surgically resected pituitary tumour under a microscope. The tumour comprises sheets of monomorphic, round to polygonal cells with central nuclei and sparse to absent reticulin network. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: nbsp; Pituitary adenoma: Pituitary adenomas are benign tumors that arise from the pituitary gland and are characterized by sheets of monomorphic, round to polygonal cells with central nuclei and a sparse to absent reticulin network Cellular monomorphism and the absence of a significant reticulin network distinguish pituitary adenomas from normal anterior pituitary parenchyma. ⁠They are well-circumscribed and encapsulated. ⁠They are the most common type of pituitary tumor and can be classified based on size as follows. Pituitary carcinoma ( Option B) : Is very rare and have malignant cells showing nuclear pleomorphism along with invasive growth and metastasis. Schwannoma (Option D) : Schwannomas are tumors of Schwann cells found along peripheral nerves. They display spindle-shaped cells in a palisading pattern and stain positive for S-100 protein. They do not arise in the pituitary gland. Craniopharyngioma (Option C): Incorrect – Shows squamous epithelium , calcification , and wet keratin , not monomorphic sheets or reticulin loss. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
nbsp;

Pituitary adenoma: 

  • Pituitary adenomas are benign tumors that arise from the pituitary gland and are characterized by sheets of monomorphic, round to polygonal cells with central nuclei and a sparse to absent reticulin network

  • Cellular monomorphism and the absence of a significant reticulin network distinguish pituitary adenomas from normal anterior pituitary parenchyma.
  • ⁠They are well-circumscribed and encapsulated. 
  • ⁠They are the most common type of pituitary tumor and can be classified based on size as follows.

 

Pituitary carcinoma(Option B): Is very rare and have malignant cells showing nuclear pleomorphism along with invasive growth and metastasis.

Schwannoma (Option D): Schwannomas are tumors of Schwann cells found along peripheral nerves. They display spindle-shaped cells in a palisading pattern and stain positive for S-100 protein. They do not arise in the pituitary gland.

 

 

Craniopharyngioma (Option C):
Incorrect – Shows squamous epithelium, calcification, and wet keratin, not monomorphic sheets or reticulin loss.

Classification of Asthma Severity

  • Post-bronchodilator FEV1: Air exhaled in one second after bronchodilator use.

    • Severe: FEV1 30-49% of predicted (Option C)

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with a copper IUD inserted 9 months ago presents with lower abdominal pain, fever (38.5°C), and no visible IUD strings. She has multiple sexual partners. On exam, she has lower abdominal tenderness. What is the most likely complication?
questions.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman with a copper IUD inserted 9 months ago presents with lower abdominal pain, fever (38.5°C), and no visible IUD strings. She has multiple sexual partners. On exam, she has lower abdominal tenderness. What is the most likely complication?
questions.solution: lanation The patient’s symptoms of fever and lower abdominal pain, along with her history of multiple sexual partners, point to the diagnosis of pelvic inflammatory disease, which is a complication of IUD use. Side effects of IUDs: Side effects of IUDs Bleeding Breakthrough bleeding is common, resolves in 1–3 months. May need iron; persistent cases may require IUD removal. Pain The most common removal cause. Managed with analgesics. Resolves in 3 months. Severe pain → rare perforation. Pelvic inflammatory disease (Option C) Presents with fever, abdominal pain, and discharge. Treatment involves broad-spectrum antibiotics. IUD removal if no improvement. 3rd generation of IUD is protective against IUD. Uterine perforation (Option B) Rare complications linked to immediate postpartum insertion or poor technique. 1st generation IUDs are associated with a higher risk of perforation. Failure of contraception ➜ pregnancy MIRENA has the lowest pregnancy rates. Abortion is legally allowed on request. If threads visible → remove and continue pregnancy with risks explained. If threads not visible → assess uterus. If no complications, IUD can be removed and pregnancy continued with risk of abortion/preterm labor. Ectopic pregnancy (Option D) Recognized by lower abdominal pain, dark vaginal bleeding, or amenorrhea. Women at high risk should avoid IUDs. Expulsion (Option A) Typically occurs within weeks of insertion or during menstruation. Higher risk in young, nulliparous, postpartum women or using 1st generation IUDs Migration of IUD Rarely causes intestinal obstruction. Diagnosed via X-ray imaging if suspected. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A researcher is interested in examining the prevalence of hypertension among adults in a city and wants to identify any associated risk factors such as age, diet, and physical activity at a single time. The researcher collects data from a large sample of adults in the city. Which type of study design is the researcher using in this scenario?
questions.stemHtml: A researcher is interested in examining the prevalence of hypertension among adults in a city and wants to identify any associated risk factors such as age, diet, and physical activity at a single time. The researcher collects data from a large sample of adults in the city. Which type of study design is the researcher using in this scenario?
questions.solution: Explanation: A cross-sectional study is used to determine the prevalence of a disease in a population at a specific time. It is also known as a snapshot of the total population. Here it is cross-sectional study because it calculates prevalence of a disease and relies on primary data, i.e., researcher collects the data himself. To assess the incidence, a Cohort study (Option A) starts by determining whether risk factors are present. Case-control study (Option C) determines whether an exposure is associated with an outcome. It starts with diseased and non-diseased. An Ecological study (Option D) compares exposure and disease frequency in a series of populations. The unit of study is population. Ecological study uses secondary data. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following statements accurately describes the Quintero staging system for Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS)?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements accurately describes the Quintero staging system for Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS)?

options.label: A
options.text: Stage I is characterized by absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery of the donor twin.

options.label: B
options.text: Stage II is defined by the presence of polyhydramnios in the recipient twin and anhydramnios in the donor twin.

options.label: C
options.text: Stage III involves critically abnormal Doppler findings in one or both twins.

options.label: D
options.text: Stage V indicates the presence of hydrops fetalis in one or both twins.

questions.answerText: Stage III involves critically abnormal Doppler findings in one or both twins.
questions.solution: Correct Answer :C) Stage III involves critically abnormal Doppler findings in one or both twins. According to Quintero Staging System for TTTS, Stage III indicates presence of abnormal doppler findings in one of both twins , such as Absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery, Reversed flow in the ductus venosus Pulsatile flow in the umbilical vein. Quintero Staging System for Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS) Stage Description Stage I (Option A ruled out) Polyhydramnios in the recipient twin (deepest vertical pocket ≥8 cm) and oligohydramnios in the donor twin (deepest vertical pocket ≤2 cm), with a visible bladder in the donor twin. Stage II (Option B ruled out) The donor twin's bladder is not visible on ultrasound, indicating severe oligohydramnios. Stage III Critically abnormal Doppler findings, such as absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery, reversed flow in the ductus venosus, or pulsatile flow in the umbilical vein in one or both twins Stage IV Presence of hydrops fetalis in one or both twins, indicating severe fetal compromise Stage V (Option D ruled out) Demise of one or both twins @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer :C) Stage III involves critically abnormal Doppler findings in one or both twins.

According to Quintero Staging System for TTTS, Stage III indicates presence of abnormal doppler findings in one of both twins, such as

  • Absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery,
  • Reversed flow in the ductus venosus
  • Pulsatile flow in the umbilical vein.


 

Quintero Staging System for Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS)

Stage

Description

Stage I (Option A ruled out)

Polyhydramnios in the recipient twin (deepest vertical pocket ≥8 cm) and oligohydramnios in the donor twin (deepest vertical pocket ≤2 cm), with a visible bladder in the donor twin.

Stage II (Option B ruled out)

The donor twin's bladder is not visible on ultrasound, indicating severe oligohydramnios.

Stage III

Critically abnormal Doppler findings, such as absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery, reversed flow in the ductus venosus, or pulsatile flow in the umbilical vein in one or both twins

Stage IV

Presence of hydrops fetalis in one or both twins, indicating severe fetal compromise

Stage V (Option D ruled out)

Demise of one or both twins

trong>American trypanosomiasis:

The given image shows Romana's sign, i.e., a swollen nodule or ‘chagoma’ at the site of infection, most commonly over the eyelids or near the mouth. This is an early sign of Trypanosoma cruzei infection, which is endemic to South America and is therefore called American trypanosomiasis.

Trypanosoma cruzei is transmitted via the bite of the Reduviid bug, or kissing bug (named so because the bite is painless).

Early symptoms are non-specific and include fever, lymphadenopathy, and the Romana sign.

If untreated, it can lead to Chaga’s disease, the manifestations of which include

  1. Dilated cardiomyopathy - heart failure (option B), arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death.
  2. Megaesophagus and megacolon (options C and D) - due to autonomic nerve destruction.

Diagnosis of acute disease is by demonstration of T cruzi trypomastigote on blood smears.

Treatment of acute disease involves Nifurtimox or Benznidazole.
Chaga’s disease is incurable and requires supportive care as appropriate.

 

Sleeping sickness:

  • This is caused by T. brucei (rhodesiense or gambiense). It is endemic to rural Africa and is transmitted by the tse tse fly. It is also known as African trypanosomiasis.
  • Early infection is non-specific, with fever, cervical lymphadenopathy (Winterbottom’s sign: posterior cervical triangle lymphadenopathy), Kerandl sign (delayed pain after a sharp blow or squeeze to soft tissue) and arthralgia, which lasts for varying lengths of time.
  • Late infection is characterized by neuropsychiatric manifestations, with sleep-wake cycle disturbance prominent.

questions.answerText: Administration of aspirin, heparin, and initiation of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)
questions.solution: The management of acute MI in pregnant women is similar to that in nonpregnant patients. The initial treatment should include aspirin and heparin to manage the thrombosis, followed by percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to revascularize the affected coronary artery. PCI is the preferred method as it is effective and safe during pregnancy. Cesarean delivery is reserved for obstetrical indications after sufficient infarct healing. Epidural analgesia is preferred for labor pain management. (Option D) Immediate Induction of Labor is not the immediate priority for managing a STEMI. (Option A) Conservative Management with Bed Rest and Observation would not address the immediate need for myocardial reperfusion and could lead to a worsening of the myocardial infarction. (Option C) @Neet_pg_bot

Management of Immune thrombocytopenic purpura in children.

questions.stemHtml: In the surgical management of soft tissue sarcoma, which of the following criteria is most appropriate for achieving optimal outcomes?

options.text: Wide local excision with a 1 cm margin

options.text: Wide local excision with a 2 cm margin

questions.answerText: Wide local excision with a 2 cm margin
questions.solution: Explanation: Wide local excision with a 2 cm margin ensures complete tumour removal while preserving function and minimising tissue loss. This approach effectively reduces the risk of local recurrence. Wide local excision with a 1 cm margin (Option A) may be inadequate for many soft tissue sarcomas, potentially leading to higher rates of local recurrence. Radical excision with removal of adjacent muscle groups (Option B): It is often overly aggressive and can lead to unnecessary functional impairment without significantly improving outcomes in most cases. Radical excision with lymph node removal (Option D) is generally not necessary for most soft tissue sarcomas, as they typically spread hematogenously rather than through lymphatics, and routine lymph node dissection is not standard practice unless there is evidence of lymph node involvement. @Neet_pg_bot

AIS is an early stage of lung cancer where abnormal glandular cells are confined to the airway lining without invasion and exhibit a “lepidic growth pattern” (or butterfly on fence pattern), spreading along intact alveolar structures without invasion. questions.solution: ata-dictid="cc20d2d7111692777201fb0caeb3f2">uptake on Tc99 pertechnetate scans because of its high mitochondrial content. Histopathological features include papillary structures, cystic spaces, oncocytic epithelial cells, and lymphoid stroma. Tc99 Pertechnetate Scan: Purpose : Assesses salivary gland function and detects abnormal areas. Hot Spot : Increased uptake of the radioactive tracer (Option D) , indicating high mitochondrial content typical of Warthin's tumour. Histopathology (HPE) (Option C): Papillary Structures: Finger-like projections extending into cystic spaces. Cystic Spaces: Fluid-filled cavities within the tumor. Oncocytic Epithelial Cells: Two layers of cells with abundant mitochondria lining the papillary and cystic areas. Lymphoid Stroma: Supporting tissue with lymphocytes and germinal centres, resembling lymph node tissue. It is best identified on imaging by its hypoechoic appearance and confirmed with FNAC (Option A): While FNAC is used for diagnosis, Warthin's tumour typically shows a "hot spot" on Tc99 pertechnetate scans due to high mitochondrial content, not just hypoechoic appearance. Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ) Homologous End Joining (HEJ) Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) Base Excision Repair (BER)
questions.stemHtml:
In their CRISPR-Cas9 experiment with a mammalian cell line, the research team observes the repair of DNA double-strand breaks. Which repair mechanisms are they most likely observing?
	Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ)
	Homologous End Joining (HEJ)
	Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER)
	Base Excision Repair (BER)
questions.solution: Explanation: In a CRISPR-Cas9 experiment , the Cas9 enzyme introduces double-strand breaks (DSBs) in DNA. The cell then uses two primary repair mechanisms for these DSBs: Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ): A quick, error-prone repair mechanism that directly ligates the broken DNA ends without a template. Commonly results in insertions or deletions (indels) , making it useful for gene knockouts . Homologous Recombination / Homologous End Joining (HEJ): A high-fidelity repair mechanism that uses a homologous DNA template (often supplied by the experimenter) to repair the break accurately. Used in gene knock-in strategies. DNA Repair Mechanisms in CRISPR Context Mechanism Role in CRISPR Repair DNA Damage Type Handled Non-Homologous End Joining Yes Double-strand breaks (DSBs) Homologous End Joining (HR) Yes Double-strand breaks (DSBs) Nucleotide Excision Repair No Bulky lesions (e.g. UV damage) Base Excision Repair No Small base damage or single-strand breaks 1, 2, 3 (NHEJ, HEJ, NER) (Option B): Incorrect because NER does not participate in double-strand break repair. 1 and 4 (NHEJ and BER) (Option C): Incorrect because BER handles single-strand lesions, not DSBs. All of the above (Option D): Incorrect because NER and BER are not involved in repairing Cas9-induced DSBs. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

In a CRISPR-Cas9 experiment, the Cas9 enzyme introduces double-strand breaks (DSBs) in DNA. The cell then uses two primary repair mechanisms for these DSBs:

  • Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ):
    A quick, error-prone repair mechanism that directly ligates the broken DNA ends without a template. Commonly results in insertions or deletions (indels), making it useful for gene knockouts.

  • Homologous Recombination / Homologous End Joining (HEJ):
    A high-fidelity repair mechanism that uses a homologous DNA template (often supplied by the experimenter) to repair the break accurately. Used in gene knock-in strategies.

DNA Repair Mechanisms in CRISPR Context

Mechanism Role in CRISPR Repair DNA Damage Type Handled
Non-Homologous End Joining Yes Double-strand breaks (DSBs)
Homologous End Joining (HR) Yes Double-strand breaks (DSBs)
Nucleotide Excision Repair No Bulky lesions (e.g. UV damage)
Base Excision Repair No

Small base damage or single-strand breaks

 

1, 2, 3 (NHEJ, HEJ, NER) (Option B):
Incorrect because NER does not participate in double-strand break repair.

1 and 4 (NHEJ and BER) (Option C):
Incorrect because BER handles single-strand lesions, not DSBs.

All of the above (Option D):
Incorrect because NER and BER are not involved in repairing Cas9-induced DSBs.

options.label: A
options.text: The rotator cuff includes the Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Subscapularis, and Teres major, which collectively aid in shoulder abduction and external rotation.

options.label: B
options.text: The Subscapularis is the only rotator cuff muscle involved in internal rotation of the humerus.

options.label: C
options.text: The Infraspinatus and Teres minor are responsible for medial rotation of the shoulder joint.

options.label: D
options.text: The rotator cuff muscles are primarily located in the anterior aspect of the shoulder joint

questions.answerText: The Subscapularis is the only rotator cuff muscle involved in internal rotation of the humerus.

The Infraspinatus and Teres minor are involved in external (lateral) rotation, not medial rotation. (Option C) The rotator cuff muscles are located primarily around the shoulder joint, with some being posterior (e.g., Infraspinatus, Teres minor) and one anterior (Subscapularis) (Option D). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the clinic by their parents reporting that their infant is not meeting developmental milestones, such as rolling over or sitting up. On examination, the infant has eczema and a noticeable musty odor. Hair and skin pigmentation appear lighter. Which of the following enzymes is deficient in this infant?
questions.stemHtml: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the clinic by their parents reporting that their infant is not meeting developmental milestones, such as rolling over or sitting up. On examination, the infant has eczema and a noticeable musty odor. Hair and skin pigmentation appear lighter. Which of the following enzymes is deficient in this infant?
questions.solution: g> Explanation: The infant’s symptoms, like failure to meet developmental milestones, eczema, a musty odor, and lighter hair and skin pigmentation, are characteristic of Phenylketonuria (PKU) . PKU is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH). This enzyme deficiency disrupts the body's ability to metabolize the amino acid phenylalanine, leading to its accumulation in the body. Deficiency in tyrosinase (Option B) causes albinism. It does not typically present with a musty odor or developmental delays. Deficiency in tyrosine aminotransferase (Option C) can cause tyrosinemia type 2, which primarily affects the eyes and skin but does not present with a musty odor or developmental delays Deficiency in 4-HPPD (Option D) is less common and typically does not include the musty odor. It causes tyrosinemia type- 3 (Hawkinsuria) with a swimming pool (chlorine) odor. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
g>

Explanation:

  • The infant’s symptoms, like failure to meet developmental milestones, eczema, a musty odor, and lighter hair and skin pigmentation, are characteristic of Phenylketonuria (PKU).
  • PKU is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH).
  • This enzyme deficiency disrupts the body's ability to metabolize the amino acid phenylalanine, leading to its accumulation in the body.

 

Deficiency in tyrosinase (Option B) causes albinism. It does not typically present with a musty odor or developmental delays.

 

Deficiency in tyrosine aminotransferase (Option C) can cause tyrosinemia type 2, which primarily affects the eyes and skin but does not present with a musty odor or developmental delays

 

Deficiency in 4-HPPD (Option D) is less common and typically does not include the musty odor. It causes tyrosinemia type- 3 (Hawkinsuria) with a swimming pool (chlorine) odor.

questions.solution: /p> The given scenario describes Patau syndrome or Trisomy 13. Clinical features and associations include Rocker-bottom feet (Seen in both trisomy 13 and trisomy 18) Severe intellectual disability Keyhole/ Coloboma (eyes) Microphthalmia, microcephaly, holoprosencephaly Cleft lip/palate Polydactyly Congenital heart disease: PDA (Patent Ductus Arteriosus) or VSD (Ventricular Septal Defect) Renal defects-Polycystic kidney disease Umbilical hernia,Omphalocele Trisomy 18 is Edward syndrome: Clinical features include a prominent occiput ( Strawberry skull ) and rocker-bottom feet (Option B ruled out) @Neet_pg_bot

/p>

The given scenario describes Patau syndrome or Trisomy 13.

Clinical features and associations include

  • Rocker-bottom feet (Seen in both trisomy 13 and trisomy 18)
  • Severe intellectual disability
  • Keyhole/ Coloboma (eyes)
  • Microphthalmia, microcephaly, holoprosencephaly
  • Cleft lip/palate
  • Polydactyly
  • Congenital heart disease: PDA (Patent Ductus Arteriosus) or VSD (Ventricular Septal Defect)
  • Renal defects-Polycystic kidney disease
  • Umbilical hernia,Omphalocele

 

Trisomy 18 is Edward syndrome: Clinical features include a prominent occiput (Strawberry skull) and rocker-bottom feet (Option B ruled out)

Using the IQ formula: IQ=(Mental Age/Chronological Age)×100 Substituting the ages: Mental Age: 9 years Chronological Age: 15 years IQ = (9/15)×100 = 60 (Options B, C, and D) Intellectual Disability Significant limitations in both: Intellectual functioning –reasoning, learning, problem-solving. Adaptive behaviour – conceptual, social, and practical skills. Onset before 18 years. Intelligence quotient Intelligence is usually measured by calculating IQ. IQ is an intelligence quotient. IQ = (Mental age ÷ Chronological age) x 100 Chronological age - Age calculated from the date of birth. Mental age - The age of one's intellect. Various tests are done to calculate mental age. Normal IQ: 90-109 Borderline IQ: 80-89 Mental retardation: IQ < 70 @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
p;

Explanation:

The child’s IQ calculated using the formula is 60, indicating significant limitations in intellectual functioning.

  1. Using the IQ formula:
    IQ=(Mental Age/Chronological Age)×100
  2. Substituting the ages:
    • Mental Age: 9 years
    • Chronological Age: 15 years
  3. IQ = (9/15)×100 = 60 (Options B, C, and D)

 

Intellectual Disability

  • Significant limitations in both:
    • Intellectual functioning –reasoning, learning, problem-solving.
    • Adaptive behaviour – conceptual, social, and practical skills.
  • Onset before 18 years.

 

Intelligence quotient

  • Intelligence is usually measured by calculating IQ.
  • IQ is an intelligence quotient.
  • IQ = (Mental age ÷ Chronological age) x 100
    • Chronological age - Age calculated from the date of birth.
    • Mental age - The age of one's intellect.
    • Various tests are done to calculate mental age.
  • Normal IQ: 90-109
  • Borderline IQ: 80-89
  • Mental retardation: IQ < 70

According to the new terminologies in NTEP, how should this patient's case be categorized?
questions.stemHtml: A 35 year old man visits the clinic with a persistent cough and fever lasting for more than 2 weeks. He also reports experiencing night sweats and significant weight loss over the past month. Sputum smear tests or radiological tests are not yet done. According to the new terminologies in NTEP, how should this patient's case be categorized?
questions.solution: TB case" according to NTEP's new terminologies as the patient is showing cough, fever or night sweats & apparent loss in weight for more than 2 weeks . The term Presumptive TB case is used in place of TB suspect (Option B) and refers to individuals who show symptoms suggestive of TB but have not yet been confirmed with a diagnosis. This term is crucial for early identification and screening of TB cases to initiate timely diagnosis and treatment. The new NTEP changes in terminologies are as follows: Category Description Criteria/Features Presumptive TB Case Used in place of TB suspect . Individuals showing symptoms suggestive of TB but not yet confirmed. Cough, Fever, Night sweats +- Weight loss > 2 weeks Clinically Diagnosed TB Case (Option A) Sputum negative but with high clinical suspicion of TB. Used in place of Sputum negative TB case. (Option C) Persistent symptoms despite negative sputum smear High clinical suspicion based on symptoms, radiological and histological features Bacteriologically Confirmed TB Case Biological specimen is positive for sputum AFB and/or CBNAAT. Used in place of Sputum positive TB case. Positive sputum smear for AFB Positive CBNAAT test confirming the presence of TB bacteria @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with a newly diagnosed left-sided breast mass on routine mammography. Core needle biopsy shows the following findings. Further molecular study revealed the involvement of the CDH1 gene. Which of the following statements are incorrect concerning this type of breast cancer? 1) Increased E-cadherin expression is observed in tumor cells. 2) Minimal desmoplasia and fibrosis were observed on microscopy. 3) A contralateral breast examination is usually required due to bilateral involvement. 4) It is associated with a poor prognosis compared to other types of breast cancer. 5) Metastatic spread affects leptomeninges and retroperitoneum.
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old woman presents with a newly diagnosed left-sided breast mass on routine mammography. Core needle biopsy shows the following findings. Further molecular study revealed the involvement of the CDH1 gene. Which of the following statements are incorrect concerning this type of breast cancer? 1) Increased E-cadherin expression is observed in tumor cells. 2) Minimal desmoplasia and fibrosis were observed on microscopy. 3) A contralateral breast examination is usually required due to bilateral involvement. 4) It is associated with a poor prognosis compared to other types of breast cancer. 5) Metastatic spread affects leptomeninges and retroperitoneum.
questions.solution: Invasive lobular breast carcinoma: CDH1 gene mutation : Decreased E-cadherin levels (also seen in signet ring gastric adenocarcinoma). (Statement 1) Clinically: Bilateral and multicentric lesions; if one breast has ILC, both breasts should be examined. (Statement 3) Microscopy Features: The tumor cells are dyscohesive, present back to back, and are called Indian file pattern. Shows minimal desmoplasia and fibrosis. (Statement 2) Metastatic spread to the retroperitoneum and leptomeninges is called carcinomatous meningitis. (Statement 5) Excellent prognosis because it usually belongs to Luminal A and B categories. (Statement 4) @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Invasive lobular breast carcinoma:

  • CDH1 gene mutation: Decreased E-cadherin levels (also seen in signet ring gastric adenocarcinoma). (Statement 1)
  • Clinically: Bilateral and multicentric lesions; if one breast has ILC, both breasts should be examined. (Statement 3)
  • Microscopy Features:
    • The tumor cells are dyscohesive, present back to back, and are called Indian file pattern.
    • Shows minimal desmoplasia and fibrosis. (Statement 2)
  • Metastatic spread to the retroperitoneum and leptomeninges is called carcinomatous meningitis. (Statement 5)
  • Excellent prognosis because it usually belongs to Luminal A and B categories.(Statement 4)

questions.solution: ong> The image shows a tissue section with the following key histological features: Branched and striated fibers Centrally located nuclei Intercalated discs (seen as dark transverse lines) One or two nuclei per cell These features are characteristic of cardiac muscle tissue . Skeletal Muscle Cardiac Muscle Smooth Muscle Longitudinal Section : Fibers are long, parallel, and non-branching . Characteristic transverse striations are visible. Multiple flat nuclei located at the periphery . Fibers are separated by connective tissue (Epimysium, perimysium, endomysium). Transverse Section : Fibers appear as irregularly round structures with peripheral nuclei. Muscle fibers are grouped into numerous fascicles. Myofibrils appear as small dots within fibers at higher magnification. Composed of individual cells with centrally placed nuclei . Displays transverse striations. Clear perinuclear halo around the nucleus. Cells are separated by intercalated discs (transverse lines). Fibers exhibit branching. Blood vessels are present. Loose connective tissue is seen above and below muscle layers. Longitudinal Section : Fibers are spindle-shaped with tapering ends . Centrally located elongated nucleus . No visible striations. Transverse Section : Spindle-shaped cells are cut at varying lengths, producing different shapes and sizes. Nuclei are visible in cells cut through the center. Cells cut away from the center do not show nuclei. Purkinje fibers (Option D): Incorrect because Purkinje fibers are a specialized type of cardiac conducting fiber , larger , pale-staining , and often lack prominent striations . They are not the dominant feature in this section. @Neet_pg_bot

The image shows a tissue section with the following key histological features:

  • Branched and striated fibers

  • Centrally located nuclei

  • Intercalated discs (seen as dark transverse lines)

  • One or two nuclei per cell

These features are characteristic of cardiac muscle tissue.

Skeletal Muscle

Cardiac Muscle

Smooth Muscle

Longitudinal Section:

  • Fibers are long, parallel, and non-branching.
  • Characteristic transverse striations are visible.
  • Multiple flat nuclei located at the periphery.
  • Fibers are separated by connective tissue (Epimysium, perimysium, endomysium).

Transverse Section:

  • Fibers appear as irregularly round structures with peripheral nuclei.
  • Muscle fibers are grouped into numerous fascicles.
  • Myofibrils appear as small dots within fibers at higher magnification.

 
  • Composed of individual cells with centrally placed nuclei.
  • Displays transverse striations.
  • Clear perinuclear halo around the nucleus.
  • Cells are separated by intercalated discs (transverse lines).
  • Fibers exhibit branching.
  • Blood vessels are present.
  • Loose connective tissue is seen above and below muscle layers.

Longitudinal Section:

  • Fibers are spindle-shaped with tapering ends.
  • Centrally located elongated nucleus.
  • No visible striations.

Transverse Section:

  • Spindle-shaped cells are cut at varying lengths, producing different shapes and sizes.
  • Nuclei are visible in cells cut through the center.
  • Cells cut away from the center do not show nuclei.

 

 Purkinje fibers (Option D):
Incorrect because Purkinje fibers are a specialized type of cardiac conducting fiber, larger, pale-staining, and often lack prominent striations. They are not the dominant feature in this section.

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man presents with knee pain and reports that he feels a "catching" sensation during movement after a recent sports injury. On examination, there is localized tenderness along the joint line, and he experiences difficulty fully extending the knee. options.label: B
options.text: Pain on passive extension of the knee

options.label: C

questions.answerText: Locking of the knee during movement
questions.solution: a-dictid="ddb3fc5499169277719282f6100904">meniscal tear is locking of the knee during movement. This symptom, along with the “catching” sensation and joint line tenderness, strongly suggests a meniscal injury Meniscal Injuries: Anatomy of the Menisci Location: Fibrocartilaginous structures between femur and tibia in the knee joint. Types: Medial Meniscus: Inner side of the knee; less mobile and more prone to injury due to capsule attachments. Lateral Meniscus: Outer side of the knee; more mobile than the medial meniscus. Structure: Composed of circumferential collagen fibers with radial strands; prone to longitudinal tears. Functions: Aids proprioception through mechanoreceptors that detect joint motion and position. Enhance joint stability and congruency. Facilitate smooth knee motion. Distribute load during weight-bearing (50% in extension; up to 90% in flexion). Mechanism of Meniscal Tears Common Causes: Rotational and Shearing Forces: Twisting a flexed knee under weight (common in sports). Age-Related Degeneration: Reduced mobility in older adults leads to tears with minimal force. Tear Mechanism by Age: Younger Individuals: Traumatic tears from specific sports incidents. Older Individuals: Tears may occur with less force due to degenerative changes, often without a distinct injury. Clinical Features of Meniscal Tears Symptom/ Feature Description Pain Localized to the joint line, particularly medial; worsens with activities stressing the meniscus. Swelling Delayed onset, usually hours after injury; presents as effusion. (Option A ruled out) Mechanical Symptoms Locking: Difficulty fully extending the knee; suggests "bucket-handle" tear. (Option C) Catching: Sensation of knee getting stuck, indicating loose fragment. Giving Way: Knee buckling during twisting movements, suggesting instability. Examination Findings Tenderness: Localized along the joint line, typically medial. Limited Extension: Difficulty achieving full knee extension. Quadriceps Wasting: Possible in chronic cases. Special Tests: Clinical tests ( McMurray's, Apley's, Thessaly) assist diagnosis; MRI is the gold standard. Pain on passive extension (Option B) is more indicative of ligamentous injuries rather than meniscal tears. Dislocation of the knee (Option D) joint is not a feature of meniscal tears; it suggests a more severe injury or instability. @Neet_pg_bot

      • Medial Meniscus: Inner side of the knee; less mobile and more prone to injury due to capsule attachments.
      • Lateral Meniscus: Outer side of the knee; more mobile than the medial meniscus.
    • Structure: Composed of circumferential collagen fibers with radial strands; prone to longitudinal tears.
    • Functions:
      • Aids proprioception through mechanoreceptors that detect joint motion and position.
      • Enhance joint stability and congruency.
      • Facilitate smooth knee motion.
      • Distribute load during weight-bearing (50% in extension; up to 90% in flexion).

    Mechanism of Meniscal Tears

    • Common Causes:
      • Rotational and Shearing Forces: Twisting a flexed knee under weight (common in sports).
      • Age-Related Degeneration: Reduced mobility in older adults leads to tears with minimal force.
    • Tear Mechanism by Age:
      • Younger Individuals: Traumatic tears from specific sports incidents.
      • Older Individuals: Tears may occur with less force due to degenerative changes, often without a distinct injury.


     

    Clinical Features of Meniscal Tears

    Symptom/ Feature

    Description

    Pain

    Localized to the joint line, particularly medial; worsens with activities stressing the meniscus.

    Swelling

    Delayed onset, usually hours after injury; presents as effusion. (Option A ruled out)

    Mechanical Symptoms
    • Locking: Difficulty fully extending the knee; suggests "bucket-handle" tear. (Option C)
    • Catching: Sensation of knee getting stuck, indicating loose fragment.
    • Giving Way: Knee buckling during twisting movements, suggesting instability.

    Examination Findings
    • Tenderness: Localized along the joint line, typically medial.
    • Limited Extension: Difficulty achieving full knee extension.
    • Quadriceps Wasting: Possible in chronic cases.
    • Special Tests: Clinical tests (McMurray's, Apley's, Thessaly) assist diagnosis; MRI is the gold standard.

     

    Pain on passive extension (Option B) is more indicative of ligamentous injuries rather than meniscal tears.

     

    Dislocation of the knee (Option D) joint is not a feature of meniscal tears; it suggests a more severe injury or instability.

questions.solution: ata-dictid="ee07cb1aaf16927771856285b258d9">CVP (3 cm H2O) suggests hypovolemia , which is consistent with the patient's tachycardia and hypotension. Administering a fluid bolus is the first-line treatment to increase preload and improve hemodynamics. Central Venous Pressure (CVP) Monitoring: CVP measures the pressure in the thoracic vena cava near the right atrium, reflecting right ventricular preload and overall fluid status. Measurement Method (Invasive): Central venous catheter placed in large veins (e.g., subclavian or internal jugular), connected to a pressure transducer Normal Range: 3-8 mmHg. Low CVP Causes: Hypovolemia (blood loss or dehydration). Venodilation (e.g., in septic shock). Elevated CVP Causes: Heart failure, fluid overload, valve dysfunction. Increased intrathoracic pressure (e.g., mechanical ventilation, tension pneumothorax). Clinical Use: Guides fluid resuscitation. Helps assess heart function and venous return. Vasopressors (Option A) may be required if hypotension persists after adequate fluid resuscitation, but not as the initial step. Blood transfusion (Option C) is not indicated unless there is evidence of blood loss or anemia. Increasing anesthetic depth (Option D) is inappropriate here, as the patient is likely hypovolemic. @Neet_pg_bot

He has a history of unprotected sexual intercourse in the past few months and reports a painless ulcer, which healed without scarring. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.answerText: Presents with an indurated ulcer and painless lymphadenopathy
questions.solution: /p> Explanation: The given clinical presentation of a male with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse , swelling in the inguinal region (inguinal lymphadenopathy) and a painless ulcer that has healed without scarring is suggestive of lymphogranuloma venerum, caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. The incorrect statement is that it presents with an indurated ulcer and painless lymphadenopathy. Lymphogranuloma venerum (LGV): It is a sexually transmitted disease caused by serovars L1-L3 of Chlamydia trachomatis (M/C strain causing LGV: L2 ). It occurs in sexually active adults of all ages. It can cause LGV-associated proctitis in homosexuals, associated with HIV and hepatitis C co-infection. The incubation period of LGV is around 3-30 days , and the disease presents in three stages, described in the table below: Primary Secondary Tertiary 3-30 days Days-weeks Years after a chronic, untreated infection Small papule/pustule/ Non-indurated ulcer at the site of inoculation which heals spontaneously with no scarring. Lymphatic involvement of nodes that drain the primary lesion. Classic form: Tender unilateral or bilateral inguinal and/or femoral adenopathy (Groove sign of Greenblatt). The lymph nodes may coalesce to form a bubo or abscesses that may rupture spontaneously with the development of Fistulae or sinus tracts. There may be systemic features such as malaise and fever. Lymphatic obstruction due to chronic inflammation leads to fistula formation, strictures, and disfiguring conditions such as genital elephantiasis and esthiomene , which refers to hypertrophic enlargement with ulceration of the external genitalia. Diagnosis of LGV can be confirmed by the Nucelic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT). Antibody detection by real-time PCR can also be done. Treatment includes: First line: Doxycycline 100mg BD x 21 days. Second line: Erythromycin 500mg 4 times a day x 21 days. Third line: Azithromycin 1g weekly once x 21 days. Caused by Chlamydia trachomatis L1-L3 (Option A): This statement is true; these specific serovars are the causative agents of LGV. Can be associated with hepatitis C co-infection (Option B): This statement is true; co-infections with other STIs, including HCV, are possible in individuals with LGV. Esthiomene is a complication in the tertiary stage of this disease (Option D): This statement is true; esthiomene (genital elephantiasis) is a recognized chronic complication of untreated or persistent LGV infection. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old professional singer presents with complaints of vocal fatigue and difficulty producing high-pitched sounds for the last 3 months. She denies any difficulty in swallowing or breathing. On laryngoscopic examination, no significant abnormalities are seen, and one vocal cord appears to be in normal resting position while other vocal cord is in abducted position . What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old professional singer presents with complaints of vocal fatigue and difficulty producing high-pitched sounds for the last 3 months. She denies any difficulty in swallowing or breathing. On laryngoscopic examination, no significant abnormalities are seen, and one vocal cord appears to be in normal resting position while other vocal cord is in abducted position . What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: SLN palsy Explanation: In this scenario, the patient is a professional singer who reports difficulty with high-pitched sounds, which is a hallmark of unilateral SLN palsy . The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve innervates the cricothyroid muscle , which tenses the vocal cords, crucial for producing high-pitched sounds. In unilateral SLN palsy, the patient does not experience breathing or swallowing difficulties, and laryngoscopic examination may appear normal. Unilateral SLN Palsy Motor Loss: Cricothyroid muscle - decreased ability to tense the vocal cord. Sensory Loss: Above the vocal cord on the affected side. Vocal Cord Position: The affected vocal cord appears shortened and wavy ; may exhibit flapping due to loss of tension. Other Features: Askew position of the glottis with the anterior commissure rotated towards the healthy side. Voice changes such as weakness and inability to raise pitch, affecting singing ability. Treatment: Primarily voice therapy to improve vocal function and manage symptoms. Bilateral SLN Palsy Motor Loss: Both cricothyroid muscles - bilateral loss of vocal cord tension. Sensory Loss: Above the vocal cords bilaterally. Vocal Cord Position: Both vocal cords may be shortened and lack tension , potentially leading to difficulties with voice production. Other Features: Inhalation of food and secretions resulting in coughing and choking . The voice is weak and husky . Treatment: Tracheostomy with a cuffed tube and esophageal feeding tube, if aspiration is severe. Epiglottopexy (reversible) - close laryngeal inlet - to protect the lungs from aspiration. Voice pitch improvement through surgical approximation of the thyroid and cricoid cartilages. Bilateral SLN palsy (Option A): The patient would have more pronounced symptoms, including a monotonous voice, significant difficulty with high-pitched sounds, and aspiration due to poor sensation in the upper larynx. Unilateral RLN palsy (Option C) Causes hoarseness and, on laryngoscopy, shows one vocal cord in a paramedian position . In contrast, this patient's difficulty is specifically related to high-pitched sounds , pointing to SLN involvement rather than RLN. Bilateral RLN palsy (Option D): It is a severe condition that typically results in stridor or significant respiratory difficulty due to both vocal cords being fixed in the paramedian position. The absence of breathing or swallowing problems in this patient rules out bilateral RLN palsy. @Neet_pg_bot

  • In unilateral SLN palsy, the patient does not experience breathing or swallowing difficulties, and laryngoscopic examination may appear normal.

 

Unilateral SLN Palsy

  • Motor Loss: Cricothyroid muscle - decreased ability to tense the vocal cord.
  • Sensory Loss: Above the vocal cord on the affected side.
  • Vocal Cord Position: The affected vocal cord appears shortened and wavy; may exhibit flapping due to loss of tension.
  • Other Features:
    • Askew position of the glottis with the anterior commissure rotated towards the healthy side.
    • Voice changes such as weakness and inability to raise pitch, affecting singing ability.
  • Treatment: Primarily voice therapy to improve vocal function and manage symptoms.

 

Bilateral SLN Palsy

  • Motor Loss: Both cricothyroid muscles - bilateral loss of vocal cord tension.
  • Sensory Loss: Above the vocal cords bilaterally.
  • Vocal Cord Position: Both vocal cords may be shortened and lack tension, potentially leading to difficulties with voice production.
  • Other Features:
    • Inhalation of food and secretions resulting in coughing and choking.
    • The voice is weak and husky.
  • Treatment:
    • Tracheostomy with a cuffed tube and esophageal feeding tube, if aspiration is severe.
    • Epiglottopexy (reversible) - close laryngeal inlet - to protect the lungs from aspiration.
    • Voice pitch improvement through surgical approximation of the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.

 

Bilateral SLN palsy (Option A):

  • The patient would have more pronounced symptoms, including a monotonous voice, significant difficulty with high-pitched sounds, and aspiration due to poor sensation in the upper larynx.

 

Unilateral RLN palsy (Option C)

  • Causes hoarseness and, on laryngoscopy, shows one vocal cord in a paramedian position.
  • In contrast, this patient's difficulty is specifically related to high-pitched sounds, pointing to SLN involvement rather than RLN.

 

Bilateral RLN palsy (Option D):

  • It is a severe condition that typically results in stridor or significant respiratory difficulty due to both vocal cords being fixed in the paramedian position.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with hypotonia, poor feeding, constipation and developmental delays. The child was born at term with a low birth weight. Which of the following conditions is most likely to be the underlying cause?
questions.stemHtml: A 6-month-old infant presents with hypotonia, poor feeding, constipation and developmental delays. The child was born at term with a low birth weight. Which of the following conditions is most likely to be the underlying cause?
questions.solution: pan> Hypothyroidism Explanation: The presenting features along with low birth weight suggests Congenital Hypothyroidism. Congenital Hypothyroidism presents with features like: Hypotonia : Low muscle tone due to inadequate thyroid hormone levels. Poor Feeding : Infants with congenital hypothyroidism often have difficulty feeding, which can result in poor weight gain. Developmental Delays : Delay in reaching developmental milestones is common, including motor and cognitive delays. Congenital hypothyroidism can be associated with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) , leading to a low birth weight. Down Syndrome (Option A) : While Down syndrome can cause developmental delays, it usually presents with characteristic features such as hypotonia and distinct facial dysmorphisms, and it is not specifically associated with low birth weight. Cerebral Palsy (Option C) : This condition often results from brain injury and might present with hypotonia, but it typically becomes apparent later and is less likely to be the cause of poor feeding and low birth weight at 6 months. Management of Locally Advanced Breast Cancer (LABC)

Stages Involved: Stage IIIA, IIIB and IIIC

  • Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy (NACT): Administered before surgery to shrink the tumor, making it operable and allowing for breast conservation if possible.
    • This also helps assess the tumor's response to treatment.

    • The surgery aims to achieve local control and address regional disease.
  • Post-Surgery Radiotherapy (RT): Administered after MRM to reduce the risk of local recurrence and ensure any remaining microscopic disease is treated.

NACT + MRM + RT is the standard approach for LABC to ensure comprehensive treatment. This sequence allows for effective tumor reduction, surgical resection, and post-operative control to prevent a recurrence.

questions.solution: ong> For impending corneal perforation, necrotic tissue is first removed (mechanical debridement), then tissue adhesive (e.g., cyanoacrylate glue) is applied to seal the thin area and prevent rupture. questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old hypertensive patient presents to the emergency department with severe chest pain and a rapid heartbeat. His blood pressure is 180/120mmHg. To manage his condition, a Phentolamine is administered. Later, he experiences an allergic reaction, and epinephrine is given to treat this condition. Which of the following best describes the Vasomotor reversal of Dale?

options.label: A
options.text: Epinephrine administration after phentolamine causes an increased blood pressure.

options.label: B
options.text: Epinephrine administration after phentolamine causes decreased blood pressure.

options.label: C
options.text: Epinephrine administration after phentolamine causes an increased heart rate.

options.label: D
options.text: Epinephrine administration after phentolamine causes decrease in heart rate.

questions.answerText: Epinephrine administration after phentolamine causes decreased blood pressure.
questions.solution: strong>Explanation: Phentolamine is a non-selective alpha-adrenergic blocker that blocks alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors, causing vasodilation and decreased peripheral resistance. When epinephrine (which acts on both alpha and beta receptors) is administered after phentolamine blockade, alpha receptors are blocked, so epinephrine’s alpha-mediated vasoconstriction is blocked. Therefore, epinephrine’s beta-2 mediated vasodilation predominates, causing vasodilation and a decrease in blood pressure (paradoxical hypotension). This phenomenon is called the Vasomotor reversal of Dale or the "epinephrine reversal" phenomenon. Epinephrine administration after phentolamine causes an increased blood pressure (Option A): Incorrect because alpha receptors are blocked, so vasoconstriction is prevented and BP decreases. Epinephrine administration after phentolamine causes an increased heart rate (Option C): Incorrect as a description of vasomotor reversal; HR does increase but the key feature is BP decrease. Epinephrine administration after phentolamine causes decrease in heart rate (Option D): Incorrect because heart rate increases due to beta-1 stimulation and reflex tachycardia. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
strong>Explanation:

  • Phentolamine is a non-selective alpha-adrenergic blocker that blocks alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors, causing vasodilation and decreased peripheral resistance.

  • When epinephrine (which acts on both alpha and beta receptors) is administered after phentolamine blockade, alpha receptors are blocked, so epinephrine’s alpha-mediated vasoconstriction is blocked.

  • Therefore, epinephrine’s beta-2 mediated vasodilation predominates, causing vasodilation and a decrease in blood pressure (paradoxical hypotension).

  • This phenomenon is called the Vasomotor reversal of Dale or the "epinephrine reversal" phenomenon.

Epinephrine administration after phentolamine causes an increased blood pressure (Option A): Incorrect because alpha receptors are blocked, so vasoconstriction is prevented and BP decreases.

Epinephrine administration after phentolamine causes an increased heart rate (Option C): Incorrect as a description of vasomotor reversal; HR does increase but the key feature is BP decrease.

Epinephrine administration after phentolamine causes decrease in heart rate (Option D): Incorrect because heart rate increases due to beta-1 stimulation and reflex tachycardia.

  • Benzodiazepines (e.g., diazepam, lorazepam, or chlordiazepoxide) are the first-line treatment as they:

    • Enhance GABAergic inhibition, reducing excitatory overactivity.

    • Prevent progression to seizures and cardiovascular complications.

    • Provide sedation and symptom control.

    Moderate Tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, hallucinations Benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam, diazepam)

    • Used only as an adjunct for persistent agitation after benzodiazepine administration.

     

    Prescribe SSRIs (Option B): Incorrect

    • SSRIs have no role in managing acute alcohol withdrawal or DTs.

    • Mood stabilization is considered after withdrawal resolution.

    • Opioid therapy is for opioid withdrawal, not alcohol withdrawal.

What is the best investigation in the workup for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 15-year-old girl presents to the clinic with concerns about not having started her menstrual periods. The urine pregnancy test was negative & the physical examination showed normal secondary sexual characteristics. Pelvic ultrasound reveals an absent uterus. What is the best investigation in the workup for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Serum FSH , LH , TSH , PRL levels

questions.solution: is Explanation: In a case where a patient presents with primary amenorrhea, normal secondary sexual characteristics, and an absent uterus on ultrasound, the patient is suspected to have Müllerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome, 46, XX) or androgen insensitivity syndrome (46, XY). Thus, the next appropriate step is to perform a karyotype analysis , which is necessary to differentiate between the two. questions.solution: rong>chronic pancreatitis, there is progressive loss of pancreatic exocrine function affecting all three major enzymes — lipase , amylase , and proteases (trypsin) . Fat malabsorption is the most clinically significant due to lipase deficiency, but protein digestion is also impaired due to reduced protease (trypsin) secretion. Therefore, enzyme replacement therapy should ideally include both lipase and protease (trypsin) to address malabsorption of fats and proteins. Amylase supplementation is generally not needed, as carbohydrate digestion is less affected and often compensated by salivary amylase and brush border enzymes. Hence, combined lipase and trypsin supplementation is more appropriate than lipase alone. Aspect Details Clinical Presentation Chronic abdominal pain, steatorrhea, weight loss, pancreatic calcifications Etiology Chronic alcohol abuse causing chronic pancreatitis Enzyme Deficiency Lipase (fat digestion), proteases like trypsin (protein digestion) Treatment Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy with lipase and protease (trypsin) Lipase only (Option A): Incorrect because protein digestion impairment also contributes to malnutrition; protease replacement improves overall digestion and nutrition. Amylase only (Option B): Incorrect because carbohydrate digestion is usually preserved; amylase replacement is unnecessary. Proteinase and amylase (Option D): Incorrect because lipase replacement is critical for fat digestion; omission of lipase would fail to treat steatorrhea. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: hronic productive cough with recurrent foul-smelling sputum and hemoptysis suggests chronic suppurative lung disease. This, along with the characteristic "tram track sign" seen on high-resolution CT, points towards a diagnosis of bronchiectasis . Radiographic Findings of Bronchiectasis: Tramline Sign/Tram track sign (Option C): Thickened bronchial walls seen as single thick lines or parallel line opacities. {{caption_text}} Cystic bronchiectasis: Multiple thin-walled ring shadows with air-fluid levels. Computed Tomographic (CT) Findings: Major sign: Bronchial dilation, with or without bronchial wall thickening. Lack of tapering of bronchial lumina. Signet ring sign: Bronchial diameter greater than the adjacent pulmonary artery. {{caption_text}} Glove-finger/V/Y-shaped densities: Represent mucus-filled dilated bronchi. Tree-in-bud sign (Option A): More commonly seen with endobronchial spread of tuberculosis. Also seen in bronchiolitis as small nodular and branching opacities. Ground-glass opacities (Option B) are hazy areas of increased lung opacity with preserved bronchial and vascular markings, typically seen in interstitial lung diseases, viral infections, or pulmonary edema, not in airway dilation. hronic productive cough with recurrent foul-smelling sputum and hemoptysis suggests chronic suppurative lung disease. This, along with the characteristic "tram track sign" seen on high-resolution CT, points towards a diagnosis of bronchiectasis.

 

Radiographic Findings of Bronchiectasis:

  • Tramline Sign/Tram track sign (Option C): Thickened bronchial walls seen as single thick lines or parallel line opacities.
  • Cystic bronchiectasis: Multiple thin-walled ring shadows with air-fluid levels.

Computed Tomographic (CT) Findings:

  • Major sign: Bronchial dilation, with or without bronchial wall thickening.
  • Lack of tapering of bronchial lumina.
  • Signet ring sign: Bronchial diameter greater than the adjacent pulmonary artery.
  • Glove-finger/V/Y-shaped densities: Represent mucus-filled dilated bronchi.
  • Tree-in-bud sign (Option A):
    • More commonly seen with endobronchial spread of tuberculosis.
    • Also seen in bronchiolitis as small nodular and branching opacities. 

 

Ground-glass opacities (Option B) are hazy areas of increased lung opacity with preserved bronchial and vascular markings, typically seen in interstitial lung diseases, viral infections, or pulmonary edema, not in airway dilation.

Air bronchogram (Option D) refers to air-filled bronchi visible within opacified alveolar regions, seen in alveolar consolidation such as pneumonia, not in bronchial wall thickening or dilation.

ustomMeta" data-dictid="488a4efe7d16927771840c9e29f164">congenital rubella is “salt and pepper” retinopathy.


 

Congenital rubella
  • Rubella (German measles) is a mild disease in infants and children but can cause congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) if contracted during pregnancy.
  • The risk is highest in the first trimester, especially within the first 8 weeks.

Pathogenesis

  • Viremia is most intense from 10 to 17 days after infection.
  • Viral shedding is from day 10 of infection up to 2 weeks.

Risk of Defects by Gestational Age
  • Highest in the first 12 weeks of gestation and decreases significantly thereafter, with defects being rare after 20 weeks.

Clinical features of congenital rubella syndrome
  • Hearing loss (most common)
  • Vision problems (cataracts, glaucoma, salt and pepper retinopathy).
    • Cataracts are the most common ocular abnormality associated with congenital rubella.

  • Heart defects (patent ductus arteriosus > pulmonary artery stenosis (right > left) > ventricular septal defect)
  • Low birth weight
  • Neurological issues (microcephaly, intellectual disabilities, encephalitis, behavioral issues)

Chronicity and Complications
  • Chronic presence of the virus can cause ongoing damage
  • The risk of progressive rubella panencephalitis (PRP) years later is a rare complication.
  • Less common complications: Growth retardation, hepatitis, bone lesions.
  • Risk of diabetes and thyroid dysfunction

Diagnosis
  • Rubella IgM enzyme immunosorbent assay (detects antibodies)
  • Viral isolation (growing the virus from samples)
  • Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (detects viral RNA)

Management
  • No specific treatment for CRS; supportive care is key
  • Early intervention for complications (e.g., hearing loss) is crucial

Prevention
  • Standard with droplet precaution in hospitalized cases
  • Rubella vaccination RA 27/3 live attenuated vaccine (MMR or MMRV with varicella) effectively prevents rubella and CRS
  • MMR vaccine has a 95% efficacy after one dose and 99% after two doses
  • Vaccination side effects: fever, rash, joint pain

Considerations for Pregnant Women
  • Immunoglobulin may be considered if pregnancy is not terminated, though it does not guarantee prevention of fetal infection

questions.solution: on: The given scenario is diagnosed as binocular diplopia most commonly caused by paralysis of extra ocular muscles (paralytic strabismus). Diplopia refers to the simultaneous perception of two images of a single object. Blowout fracture (Option A): Causes mechanical restriction (commonly inferior rectus entrapment → limitation of upgaze). History of trauma would be present. Thick pterygium (Option B) : Can cause restricted ocular motility but is progressive and gradual, not sudden diplopia. Subluxation of lens (Option C) : Produces monocular diplopia (persists even when one eye is closed). Not gaze-dependent, unlike this case. @Neet_pg_bot

on:

  • Subluxation of lens (Option C): Produces monocular diplopia (persists even when one eye is closed). Not gaze-dependent, unlike this case.

options.label: A
options.text: Suicide attempts were decriminalised as per IPC Section 309

options.label: B

questions.answerText: Suicide attempts were decriminalised as per IPC Section 309
questions.solution: on: Prior to the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 Indian Penal Code (IPC) Section 309: Attempting suicide was historically a criminal offence in India, punishable by imprisonment, fine, or both. This criminalisation treated suicide attempts as violations of law rather than issues of mental health. Change with the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 Section 115 explicitly states that individuals who attempt suicide shall not be punished under IPC Section 309. (Option B ruled out) Instead, they are presumed to be experiencing severe stress linked to mental illness (Option C ruled out) and should receive care, treatment, and rehabilitation to prevent recurrence. This shift promotes a compassionate, health-centric approach , emphasizing the need for psychiatric help rather than imprisonment. Mental healthcare professionals are now mandated to provide appropriate psychosocial support and treatment for underlying mental health conditions. This act also helps reduce the stigma associated with mental illness, encouraging individuals to seek help without fear of legal repercussions. (Option D ruled out) @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: /p> A positive Jones Test 2 indicates that the fluorescein dye was able to enter the lacrimal sac but could not reach the nasal cavity without syringing. This finding is typical of a partial blockage somewhere along the lacrimal drainage system, allowing some tear flow but not enough for normal drainage. Jones Test 1: Purpose : To distinguish between partial obstruction and excessive tear production. Procedure : Fluorescein dye is placed in the conjunctival sac, and after 5 minutes, a cotton bud soaked in anaesthetic is placed in the inferior meatus inside the nose. The cotton bud is checked for dye. Interpretation: Positive: Dye on the cotton bud indicates patent tear drainage and suggests hypersecretion. Negative: No dye indicates potential drainage issues, requiring further testing with Jones Test. Jones Test 2: Purpose: Performed if Jones Test 1 is negative to differentiate between partial obstruction and pump failure. Procedure: Lacrimal syringing is done while the cotton bud remains in the nose. Interpretation: Positive: Dye flushed onto the cotton bud indicates partial obstruction. Negative: No dye suggests lacrimal pump failure. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solutionHtml:
6927771874c5d97065a">erectile disorder allows for erections in specific circumstances.

 

Erectile Dysfunction

  • Incidence increases with age; reported in 2-8% of young adults and is more common in older men.
  • Not universal in aging; factors like having a partner and consistent sexual activity are protective. (Option A)
  • Episodes of erectile disorder can increase anxiety in future sexual encounters.

 

Causes:

  • Organic Causes: Due to medical conditions or medications.
    • Medical Conditions: Cardiovascular diseases (hypertension, atherosclerosis, coronary artery disease), Diabetes mellitus, Neurological disorders (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, spinal cord injuries), Endocrine disorders (hypogonadism, hyperprolactinemia, thyroid dysfunction), Chronic kidney disease, Liver cirrhosis, Pelvic or prostate surgeries, Sleep disorders (obstructive sleep apnea).
    • Medications: Antihypertensives (beta-blockers, thiazide diuretics), Antidepressants (SSRIs, tricyclic antidepressants), Antipsychotics (typical and atypical), Anti-androgens (finasteride, spironolactone), Opioids, Chemotherapy agents, Anticonvulsants, H2-receptor antagonists (cimetidine).
  • Psychogenic Causes: More common in young and middle-aged men; often related to psychological factors such as fear, anxiety, or relationship issues. (Option D)

 

Types of Male Erectile Disorder:

  1. Lifelong Male Erectile Disorder:
    • Never able to achieve an erection sufficient for insertion. (Option B)
    • Rare, occurring in about 1% of men under 35.
  2. Acquired Male Erectile Disorder:
    • Previously able to achieve penetration but later unable to do so.
    • Affects 10-20% of all men.
  3. Situational Male Erectile Disorder:
    • Able to have erections in certain situations (e.g., with a sex worker) but not with a partner.

 

Investigations used to record nocturnal erections are:

  • Nocturnal penile tumescence
  • Penile plethysmography (which measures blood pressure in the penis).

These are used to differentiate between organic and psychogenic erectile dysfunction.

 

Treatment of Erectile Dysfunction

Pharmacotherapy

Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (PDE-5 inhibitors)

  • Nitric oxide enhancers- facilitates blood flow into the penis and enhances erection.
  • Drugs- Sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil and Avanafil.
  • Not used along with organic nitrates- Can cause sudden fall in blood pressure and can be fatal. (Option B)

Other medications:

  • Oral phentolamine: May reduce sympathetic tone and relax muscles of corpora cavernosa and subsequently improve the erection.
  • Alprostadil contains naturally occurring prostaglandin E (vasodilating agent).
  • Alprostadil- Directly injected into corpora cavernosa or given intraurethral through a cannula as a pellet.

Psychotherapy

Dual sex therapy:

  • It was derived by Masters and Johnson.
  • It is also effective for other sexual disorders as well.
  • It means it treats the couple (not individual). Both the partners are involved in the treatment.
  • Couples are taught: To improve their communication and Exercises to increase sensory awareness.

Sensate focus exercises:

  • It has two stages:
  • Non-genital sensate focus: Couples should touch, rub, or kiss each other body parts excluding breasts, and genitals
  • Genital sensate focus: Stage II Involves only breasts and genitals. Subsequently, the couple can engage in complete intercourse.
  • Purpose of exercises is to make the couple aware that pleasure can be given and received by methods other than sexual intercourse (penetration).

Others:

  • Behavioral therapy
  • Hypnotherapy
  • Psychoanalysis

Examination reveals a white forelock and V-shaped leukoderma on the mid-forehead. Small spots of hyperpigmentation are also noted within the hypopigmented lesions. options.label: A
options.text: Heterozygous mutations in the KIT gene

options.label: B

questions.answerText: Heterozygous mutations in the KIT gene
questions.solution: given clinical scenario of hypopigmented macules with white forelock and V-shaped leukoderma on the forehead is suggestive of piebaldism . It is associated with heterozygous mutations in the KIT gene. Piebaldism is a rare autosomal dominant disorder with congenital white patches that results from impairment of melanoblast migration in embryonal development. The KIT gene encodes for the c-KIT protein , a receptor with tyrosine kinase activity, essential for various cellular processes, including melanocyte migration and proliferation, and throughout life. When mutations occur in one allele of the KIT gene, it disrupts the normal function of c-KIT, leading to impaired melanocyte migration and proliferation. This disruption leads to the formation of hypopigmented patches on the skin, which occur due to the absence of melanocytes in certain areas. The forehead , chest, abdomen, and extremities are typically involved. The distribution of the lesions remains for the entire life of affected individuals. The TERT gene (Option B) encodes for telomerase reverse transcriptase , which plays a crucial role in maintaining telomere length and genomic stability. Mutations in TERT have been associated with various conditions such as dyskeratosis congenita . However, there is no established association between mutations in the TERT gene and piebaldism. The SNAI2 gene (Option C) encodes for the zinc finger transcription factor Snail family transcriptional repressor 2 (SNAI2), also known as SLUG. SNAI2 is involved in various cellular processes, including epithelial-mesenchymal transition and embryonic development. There is no known association between SNAI2 mutations and piebaldism. Autosomal recessive mutations in the NOLA3 (Option D) gene are incorrect, as piebaldism typically follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. @Neet_pg_bot

    • The KIT gene encodes for the c-KIT protein, a receptor with tyrosine kinase activity, essential for various cellular processes, including melanocyte migration and proliferation, and throughout life.
    • When mutations occur in one allele of the KIT gene, it disrupts the normal function of c-KIT, leading to impaired melanocyte migration and proliferation.
    • This disruption leads to the formation of hypopigmented patches on the skin, which occur due to the absence of melanocytes in certain areas.
    • The forehead, chest, abdomen, and extremities are typically involved.
    • The distribution of the lesions remains for the entire life of affected individuals.

    The SNAI2 gene (Option C) encodes for the zinc finger transcription factor Snail family transcriptional repressor 2 (SNAI2), also known as SLUG.

    • SNAI2 is involved in various cellular processes, including epithelial-mesenchymal transition and embryonic development.
    • There is no known association between SNAI2 mutations and piebaldism.

Which diagnostic test is most useful for assessing the extent of her condition and guiding surgical planning?
questions.stemHtml: A 45 year out female presents with persistent ear discharge, hearing loss, and a feeling of fullness in the ear. Upon examination, the otolaryngologist performs an otoscopic examination, which reveals an abnormal growth in the ear canal. Which diagnostic test is most useful for assessing the extent of her condition and guiding surgical planning?
questions.solution: l> Based on the symptoms described-persistent ear discharge, hearing loss, a feeling of fullness in the ear, and the finding of abnormal growth in the ear canal, the most probable diagnosis is a cholesteatoma. High-resolution CT (HRCT) is critical for assessing the severity of the cholesteatoma, evaluating any osseous damage, and aiding in surgical planning. HRCT provides detailed imaging of bony structures and helps identify the extent of the cholesteatoma. Investigations for cholesteatoma: Otoscopic Examination: Direct inspection of the eardrum using otoscopy, video-otoscopy, otomicroscopy, or video-telescopy. Radiological Examination: CT Scan : Primary imaging technique to assess disease severity, osseous damage, and malformations. High-resolution CT (HRCT) is often used before surgery. MRI : Provides detailed tissue distinction with different pulse sequences. Cholesteatomas typically appear hyperintense on T2WI and hypointense/isointense on T1WI. Tympanometric and Audiometric Tests: Assess hearing loss; audiometry identifies conductive deficiencies. Rinne’s and Weber's tests differentiate between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss. Cholesteatoma is diagnosed using a combination of otoscopic examination, CT, MRI, and ancillary tests like tympanometry and audiometry. Video-Otoscopy (Option A) is useful for visualizing the ear canal and eardrum directly but does not provide detailed information on the extent of disease or bony structures. Rinne Test (Option C) is an audiometric test used to differentiate between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss but does not provide information on the extent of cholesteatoma or guide surgical decisions. Diffusion-weighted MRI (Option D) helps detect recurrence or residual cholesteatoma, particularly after surgery, but HRCT is the primary imaging tool for pre-surgical assessment of the disease extent. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department with an open tibial fracture following a motorcycle accident. The wound is 4 cm long with moderate soft tissue damage but no flaps or avulsions. After an initial assessment, what is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient's injury?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department with an open tibial fracture following a motorcycle accident. The wound is 4 cm long with moderate soft tissue damage but no flaps or avulsions. After an initial assessment, what is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient's injury?
questions.solution: gement protocol of open fractures, wound debridement and irrigation are crucial initial steps in the emergency care phase. This process helps to remove contaminants and devitalized tissue, reducing the risk of infection and promoting proper healing . Management of Open fractures I: Emergency Care Control bleeding Wound care: Wash the wound under strict aseptic conditions with clean tap water or saline. Cover with sterile dressing. Splinting: Apply a splint to immobilize the fracture and prevent further soft tissue damage. Antibiotics & Tetanus prophylaxis Pain management Imaging: Perform X-rays to evaluate the fracture and to plan further treatment. II: Definitive Care Wound debridement: Perform thorough debridement of all devitalized tissue. This may need to be repeated. Fracture reduction & stabilization: External fixation: Provides stability and permits access to soft tissues. Useful for severe soft tissue injuries. Internal fixation: Used for more stable fractures. Becoming more common in trauma centers. Plaster immobilization: For cases with moderate-size wounds where stable reduction can be achieved. Wound closure: Primary closure: For clean wounds debrided within 6-8 hours. Delayed primary closure: For doubtful wounds, observe for 2-3 days before closing. Secondary intention: For infected wounds or extensive soft tissue damage. Bone grafting: May be necessary for bone loss or to promote union. Vascular repair: If vascular injury is present, repair is crucial for limb salvage. III: Rehabilitation Early mobilization Joint exercises & muscle strengthening Functional rehabilitation: Gradually increase weight-bearing and return to normal activities as healing progresses. Management of open fractures based on grade: Grade 1 is managed like closed fracture. Grade 2 and 3a if clean and less than 6 hrs manage like closed, otherwise open fracture. Grade 3b and 3c are managed like open fracture. Internal fixation (Option A) is typically performed after proper wound care and assessment of the fracture and soft tissue damage. It falls under the definitive care phase. It is done for grade 1 and 2 and 3A less than 6hrs with clean wounds. While splinting (Option B) is important, it comes after wound care and is not the most appropriate next step for an open fracture. Administration of tetanus prophylaxis (Option D) is important but not the most immediate next step. It should be given as part of emergency care, but wound debridement and irrigation take precedence. @Neet_pg_bot

    II: Definitive Care

    • Wound closure:
      • Primary closure: For clean wounds debrided within 6-8 hours.
      • Delayed primary closure: For doubtful wounds, observe for 2-3 days before closing.

    • Bone grafting: May be necessary for bone loss or to promote union.

Malignant Pheochromocytoma

Tumors that have undergone metastasis to Lymph-node (or) Distant site (Biochemically same as Pheochromocytoma)

Survival Rate

5-year survival ranges from 20% to 45%.

Criteria of Malignancy

Malignancy is defined by the development of metastases

Common Sites of Metastasis

Axial skeleton, lymph nodes, liver, lung, and kidney. (Option A,C,D)

Diagnosis

  • MIBG & Gallium Dotate is Best for Diagnosis
  • Biopsy & FNAC are avoided in Malignant Pheochromocytoma
  • Confirmed by the presence of metastases in locations where neuroectodermal tissues are not normally found.
  • This is the primary criterion distinguishing malignant pheochromocytomas from benign ones, as histopathologic features alone are not reliable in predicting malignancy.

Histopathologic Criteria

No histopathologic criteria can accurately predict the clinical course of malignancy.

Primary Treatment

Surgical resection, even if not curative, can offer significant palliative benefits by managing mass effects and reducing catecholamine excess.

Response to Radiotherapy/Chemotherapy

Minimal response to radiotherapy and chemotherapy.
